name: ExtrusionStudio
type: Plant Data Acquisition / Python, Modbus TCP, Raspberry Pi
summary:
A plant-wide measurement and production system for filament extrusion lines. One server reads every line's tri-axial laser gauge over Modbus TCP, charts it live, logs every spool, prints its labels and certificate, and runs the screens around the plant on Raspberry Pis.

It began as a LabVIEW proof of concept that established the Modbus communication. Once that worked, I rebuilt the whole program from scratch in Python so it could keep up with faster production, add a calibration step that makes each spool's record accurate, and take control of every device on the floor: the lines' screens, the projector and the TVs power on an hour into the workday and off at the end of it.

bullets.text: Replaced three LabVIEW executables polling one line each with one Python service that reads every line concurrently at 20 Hz, so a powered-down line never stalls the others.
Added a calibration phase that times the filament from the laser to the spool, so each reading is logged onto the spool it is actually wound on.
Every spool gets a CSV, a serial, a QR label and an HTML certificate; the packing bench approves, inspects or rejects it and prints spool, box and master case labels.
emphasis: QR label and an HTML certificate

bullets.text: Raspberry Pi kiosks run the projector, a touch screen per line, the packing bench and a statistics TV, and the server switches them on and off with the work hours, pairing with the TV over the network.
emphasis: switches them on and off with the work hours

additionalInfo.title: ExtrusionStudio
additionalInfo.subtitle: From a LabVIEW proof of concept to a plant-wide production system
additionalInfo.problem: Three extrusion lines each had a tri-axial laser gauge, and the only record of a spool's diameter was whatever an operator wrote down. Production was speeding up, and the plant needed every reading captured, every spool judged against its tolerance, and the result visible to the operator, the packing bench and management at once.
additionalInfo.rootCause: The first version, in LabVIEW, proved the Modbus TCP communication and the register decoding. It was built as one program compiled three times, one per line, each polling on a hard-coded delay with the line's address fixed in the code. That was fine as a proof of concept and wrong as a plant system: a line could not be added without a rebuild, a dead line held up the others, and nothing it measured was tied to a spool.
constraints: Read every line concurrently at 20 Hz, with a dead line never stalling a healthy one
Tie every reading to the spool it is physically wound on, not the one on the winder when the laser saw it
Run on a headless Debian server with screens that have no computer of their own
Work with no internet on the floor: no CDN, no build step, the guides served by the server itself
Power the screens, projector and TVs with the work hours to let the lines heat up and save power overnight
approach: Rewrote the program in Python as one service: one asyncio poller and one Modbus session per line, a hub that keeps the ring buffer and statistics, and Server-Sent Events to every browser
Split the user interface into panels for each audience, each its own process, with only Admin Settings allowed to talk to the gauges
Added a calibration phase on the line station that times the filament from the laser to the spool and delays logging by that offset
Logged every spool to its own CSV and a SQLite run table, issued it a Spool SN and a serial, and wrote an HTML certificate on approval
Built the packing bench workflow: approve, inspect or reject, reasons on the serial, and spool, box and master case labels on a thermal printer
Deployed Raspberry Pi kiosks that boot straight to their page, check in with the server, and are updated, configured and power-switched from Server Settings
designDecisions: Server-Sent Events rather than WebSockets: data flows one way and SSE reconnects by itself
The poll rate is per-line configuration with a floor, because the right value depends on the PLC's response time
Each frame carries min, max and last per channel, so a spike between frames still shows on the chart
A hand-written Modbus simulator that shares no code with the client, so a test cannot hide the same bug twice
A Vizio TV cannot be woken over HDMI-CEC, so the Pi pairs with it by PIN and switches it over the network instead
The server runs whichever git branch is checked out and updates itself daily, so a test branch can be tried on the real server
impact: Every spool off every line has a record, a serial, a label and a certificate
The whole plant sees production and alarms on the projector and the statistics TV
The packing bench decides spools against the gauge's figures instead of by eye
Screens come on an hour into the workday and go off at the end of it without anyone touching them
Testing the Pi fleet drove a tool of its own, BulkSSH, to reach every Pi at once

walkthrough.title: A tour of the panels
walkthrough.intro: Everything runs on one server. Each panel is a page it serves, and each screen around the plant is a Raspberry Pi that only displays one of them. Step through them in the order the plant uses them, from the operator at the line to the people looking after the server. Every capture is from the program's own simulator with made-up spools; no plant data is on this site.

steps.title: Operator-GUI
steps.audience: The operator, one touch screen per line
body: This is how the operator controls each line on its own. The screen is locked to its line, so there is nothing to choose: the live diameter, whether it is in spec, and the three things an operator does. Start logging opens a spool; Next spool closes it and opens the next; Stop logging ends the run.

Calibrate offset is the calibration phase. A countdown ends, the operator marks the filament at the laser, and presses stop when the mark reaches the spool. From then on every reading is logged that many seconds late, so it lands on the spool it is physically wound onto rather than the one that was on the winder when the laser saw it.

body: The Operator-GUI's settings drive this read-only view. It shows every line at once on a projector over the floor: a strip chart of the last few minutes with the tolerance band, and the live X, Y, Z and average readings with each one's minimum and maximum for the spool.

Anyone on the floor can see production and spot an alarm from across the room. A line that goes out of spec turns red with a timer counting how long it has been out, and the chart keeps the excursion visible until the operator resets it.

steps.title: Packaging Panel
body: Once a spool comes off a line, the operators deal with it here. A spool that stayed in spec waits as Pending; one that went out is marked Inspect and counts as rejected until somebody looks at it. The bench opens the spool, reads its figures, and approves or rejects it. Approving a spool that went out of spec asks for a reason, whose letter goes on the end of the serial.

Approval writes the certificate and unlocks the labels: the spool label with its QR code, the spool box label, and the master case label for a box of up to five spools. The panel also carries the week's approved spools against last week, the posted production schedule, the plant environment, and each line's filament settings, which the bench confirms once a day before the first spool is decided.

steps.title: Server Settings
body: The bare-metal side of the server. It is the one process started at power-on, and it starts every other panel as a child process: start, stop and restart them, switch each one's network access, and read its output. The Devices page is every Raspberry Pi around the plant, checking in every 30 seconds: what each one shows, its screen's resolution and rotation, the sensors wired to it, its TV pairing, and a power button per screen.

It also holds the users and their roles, the Spool Manager for every spool ever logged, the server's files, the audit log of who opened which panel and changed what, and the daily update that pulls the running branch at 04:00.

steps.title: Admin Settings
body: Where management looks after the plant rather than the machine. Plant Deployment shows every floor screen live on one page, so a supervisor can see the projector, a line station, the packing bench and the dashboard without walking the floor, and change any of them from here. The other tabs plan the production schedule and post it to the floor, set display, chart and work-hour settings, troubleshoot a gauge by reading its registers, manage logging and materials, and add users.

The Spool Manager lists every spool with its line, batch, duration, readings and share in spec, filtered by status, with a search by Spool SN or batch number. Every change made anywhere is written to the audit log with who made it.

name: BulkSSH
summary:
A Windows app for working with many SSH devices at once: servers, Raspberry Pis, routers and switches. Add a list of addresses, enter the username once, and every device opens in a grid of live terminals.

I built it to speed up testing the ExtrusionStudio deployment, where every change to the Pi image had to be tried on every Pi. Mirrored keystrokes type into every ticked device, and a broadcast runs one command on all of them and shows each one's output and exit code.

images.alt: BulkSSH demo video: adding several Pis, mirroring keystrokes and broadcasting a command
images.caption: BulkSSH in use: adding several Pis, mirroring keystrokes and broadcasting a command

bullets.text: Grid of live terminals, paged when there are more devices than fit, with a full-size focus view for vim and top.
Risky commands such as reboot or rm -r need confirming before they reach several devices, and host keys are never accepted silently.
Saved passwords are optional and encrypted with the Windows account; dropped connections reconnect by themselves.

additionalInfo.title: BulkSSH
additionalInfo.subtitle: One window for every Pi on the floor
additionalInfo.problem: Testing ExtrusionStudio's Pi kiosks meant repeating the same commands on every Pi, one SSH window at a time, after every change to the image.
constraints: Add many devices in one go and connect them with one password
Never send a destructive command to several devices without confirming
Install for one user with no admin rights, or run as a single portable file
approach: Electron and TypeScript, with a grid of live terminals and a focus view
Mirror keystrokes to every ticked device, or broadcast a command and collect each exit code
Fake SSH devices for development, so the app can be tried without hardware
impact: A change to the Pi image is tried on every Pi in one pass
Released as an installer and a portable executable
Telnet, serial and SFTP transfer are next

name: RB's Auto App Updater
summary: A one-line install that puts an App Auto Updater shortcut on a Windows desktop. It checks every installed application with WinGet, shows what can be updated, and upgrades each package on its own so a single failure never stops the rest.
status: Install using this powershell command: ``` irm https://www.rileybeenders.com/AutoWinUpdater | iex ```

images.alt: This demonstrate the entire process. From installing the script to running it the first time. It takes ~30 seconds to do everything.

bullets.text: Runs the upgrades through an elevated scheduled task, so after the one-time setup the desktop shortcut updates everything without a UAC prompt.
Translates WinGet exit codes into plain-language statuses such as security blocked, manual update, restart needed, and application in use, and retries per-user installers without elevation.
Keeps itself current: every launch checks a version manifest on GitHub, downloads the newer script, and verifies its SHA-256 hash before installing.

additionalInfo.title: RB's Auto App Updater
additionalInfo.subtitle: One shortcut that keeps every app on a Windows PC up to date
additionalInfo.problem:
I use CachyOS on my laptop and have grown pretty fond of the auto-updater built into the OS. After working with Winget on Windows for a few months, I started wondering why updating applications still felt so manual.

The goal of this project was simple: create a tool that can update all supported applications on a Windows system with a single double-click. Similar to the update experience I had grown used to on Linux.

No commands to remember. No terminal interaction. Just launch it and let it handle the updates.
additionalInfo.rootCause:
Keeping applications updated on Windows can become tedious, especially when different programs use completely different update methods.

Some applications update themselves, some rely on Microsoft Store and others prompt you to visit a website, download a new `.exe`, and manually run the installer.

When you have dozens of applications installed, that fragmented process becomes unnecessarily time-consuming.
constraints: Install with one PowerShell line and no other tooling
Ask for administrator approval once, at setup, and never again
Keep going when a single package fails
Update itself safely from a public repository
approach: Split the tool into a non-elevated launcher in the user's profile and protected worker scripts in Program Files that a registered scheduled task runs with highest privileges
List available upgrades with WinGet, confirm once, then upgrade each package individually with live progress and elapsed time
Map WinGet exit codes to a friendly explanation and a next action: retry per-user installers without elevation, and flag security blocks, required restarts, and applications still in use
Check version.json on every launch and install a newer AutoAppUpdater.ps1 only after its SHA-256 hash matches the manifest
designDecisions: Convert the repository's icon.png into a multi-size .ico so the desktop shortcut looks like an app rather than a script
Explain failures in plain language instead of WinGet exit codes
impact: Installs from rileybeenders.com/AutoWinUpdater with a single PowerShell line
One double-click updates every WinGet-managed application with no UAC prompt
Failed packages are classified and skipped instead of halting the run
Detailed logs in %LOCALAPPDATA%\WingetUpdater make remote troubleshooting possible

name: Unified Ubiquiti Network
summary:
A series of cloud gateways that I have been setting up across our company, my personal home and my parents house. The setup shown in the before vs after is the "Proteor" network. My first deployment of a Unifi gateway that was recently reworked after adding cables over the past few  years. 

The "Proteor" network is planned to get an upgrade into the Fortinet system as our needs internally are growing.

images.caption: Before and After of the 'Proteor' Networ

additionalInfo.title: Unifi Network
additionalInfo.problem: I wanted enterprise-grade networking capabilities without the steep learning curve, high upfront costs, and ongoing subscription or licensing fees typically associated with traditional enterprise solutions. I also needed a platform that could reliably support and centrally manage separate networks at my home, my parents’ home and my workplace.
additionalInfo.rootCause: Our consumer-grade Google Mesh network could not reliably handle the growing number of devices at work. As production expanded, multiple machines coming online simultaneously would sometimes be assigned the same IP address, creating conflicts and disrupting connectivity. The system did not consistently detect or resolve these conflicts, showing that we had outgrown the capabilities of the existing network.
constraints: Avoid costly subscriptions, recurring licensing fees, and excessive upfront costs.

Provide centralized and reliable control over IP address assignment, network configuration, DNS, VLANs, port forwarding, and other essential networking services without introducing unnecessary complexity.
Minimize downtime and connectivity disruptions.
Provide better visibility and control than a consumer-grade mesh system.
Centrally manage multiple independent locations, including my home, my parents’ home, and my workplace.
approach: Use VLANs to separate production equipment, work devices, and IoT devices for improved security and network management.
Use monitoring and network visibility tools to identify connectivity problems and resolve them more quickly.
Adopt the platform gradually, learning enterprise networking concepts without taking on the complexity of traditional enterprise solutions.
Use UniFi’s centralized interface to configure and monitor each location remotely.
impact: Reduced IP conflicts and network-related downtime.
Greater scalability as new devices and equipment are added.
Improved security by separating production, work, and IoT devices with VLANs.

name: THE KRAKEN
summary: A 1 x 2 x 1.5 m hybrid pellet-and-filament gantry printer built for a client producing the world's largest 3D-printed statue.

post.author: Michael Gorski
post.text:
Finally, after more long nights, early mornings, weekends, and more stress on the team than I would like to admit, the Filament Innovations team wrapped up the custom KRAKEN 3D Printer build. Utilizing all the hardware we could pack in her from DYZE DESIGN (Pulsar FGF and Typhoon High-Flow FDM), the custom build with a 4x8x4ft print area (with a bed leveling flatness of 560 microns at 100C bed temp) is 99% done, minus some odds and ends. Steven Fritzinger would roll in a 3am to start powder coating and I know Riley Beenders would burn the midnight oil on the CAD work, but those guys and the entire team put in the wrench time to get her done. Here, our electrical engineer, Riley Beenders is standing in the machine to show its true scale, because as DIVE DESIGN told us yesterday (who stopped by the shop to see her), pictures of the machine only do not do her justice. Special thanks to Will Drakas who was with us in August as an intern and helped get the frame built and aligned. She will be shipping on 10/20 to her new owner Atomic Props and Effects where they are going to do some massive pellet prints for their business!
